import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Polynomial-time computability of factoring

This file formalizes the open problem of whether natural number / integer factorization can be computed in
polynomial time on a deterministic classical Turing machine.

More precisely, it formalizes the following statement:
Can the prime factorization of a natural number be computed in polynomial time
(on a deterministic classical Turing machine)?

*References:*
- [Wikipedia: List of unsolved problems in computer science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_computer_science)
- [Wikipedia: Integer factorization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_factorization)

-/

namespace PolyTime

open ComplexityTheory


/--
**The integer factorization problem**: Can the prime factorization of a positive integer
be computed in polynomial time?

We state the problem by asking if `Nat.primeFactorsList` is polynomial-time computable
(assuming typical encodings of ℕ and List ℕ into bitstrings).

*Reference:* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_factorization) -/
@[category research open, AMS 68]
theorem isPolyTime_primeFactorsList : answer(sorry) ↔ IsPolyTime Nat.primeFactorsList := by
  sorry

end PolyTime

reformulations.difference: The source asks for polynomial-time integer factorization of positive integers; Lean asks for polynomial-time computation of the particular sorted, multiplicity-preserving function Nat.primeFactorsList on all naturals, including 0.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: On positive inputs, Nat.primeFactorsList is exactly the sorted list of primes whose product is the input. An integer with b binary digits has at most b prime factors counted with multiplicity, so sorting and converting between repeated factors and prime-power notation require only polynomial overhead. A polynomial-time nontrivial-factor algorithm also yields full prime factorization through O(b) recursive splits, using polynomial-time primality testing; conversely the full list supplies a factor on composite inputs. The inferred encodings are little-endian binary for naturals and concatenated self-delimiting blocks for lists, polynomial-time equivalent to conventional binary representations. The additional input 0 is encoded by the empty string and has output []; it can be handled separately without changing polynomial-time computability. The value at 1 is the source’s empty factorization. The full complexity equivalence was not formalized, but the sorted-factorization characterization and list-encoding length formula were proved in the scratch file.

review.notes: Reviewed the sole theorem and its underlying definitions. IsPolyTime existentially quantifies one deterministic finite-state stack machine and one polynomial bound, uniformly over all inputs, measured in encoded input length; it does not assert that the recursive Lean implementation runs in polynomial time. The answer(sorry) is correctly scoped as a yes/no placeholder. Both cited Wikipedia pages still record the classical problem as open. /workspace/review/scratch.lean compiles successfully and contains encoding evaluations, boundary tests, and proofs of sorted_factorization_spec and list_encoding_length; those proofs do not use the conjecture or sorry.
